narrative:
The model determined that you have a 97% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process heavily weighs this predicted outcome, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile of your class is far below the average of accepted students, who typically rank near the middle. This low ranking signaled to the model a pattern associated with struggling on the bar exam.

Your LSAT score of 25 was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure. This score sits well below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, indicating the model saw it as a significant risk for not passing the bar.

Your first-year class rank came third. Like your third-year rank, being in the lowest decile here further reinforced the likelihood of failure, again well below the average rank of accepted students.

While your undergraduate GPA of 3.60 is actually stronger than the accepted-student average of 3.23, and your middle-income background and full-time status are fairly typical, these positive or neutral signals were not enough to overcome the dominant negative signals from your class ranks and LSAT.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to reach a more competitive score. Strengthening these key areas will directly address what the model viewed as your biggest barriers. (248 words)
